slides.title: Timing also matters
slides.text: Timing also matters Hebbian plasticity is not determined only by whether two neurons are active. The relative timing of presynaptic and postsynaptic activity can also determine the direction of plasticity. This principle is called spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP). Pre before post At many synapses, presynaptic activity shortly before postsynaptic firing favors potentiation . Post before pre At many synapses, the reverse order favors depression . The precise timing rules and time windows vary across synapses and circuits.

slides.title: Spike-timing-dependent plasticity
slides.text: Spike-timing-dependent plasticity STDP converts temporal relationships between neurons into long-lasting changes in synaptic efficacy. A synapse that consistently helps drive the postsynaptic neuron can become stronger. A synapse whose activity is poorly timed relative to postsynaptic firing can become weaker.

slides.title: From early plasticity to consolidation
slides.text: From early plasticity to consolidation A rapidly induced synaptic change is not necessarily permanent. Early phase modification of existing proteins receptor trafficking changes in synaptic efficacy primarily functional Consolidated / late phase altered gene transcription new protein synthesis stabilization of receptor changes spine remodeling formation or elimination of synaptic contacts Long-lasting plasticity can therefore progress from functional modification to structural stabilization .

slides.title: Structural plasticity
slides.text: Structural plasticity Long-lasting changes in experience can remodel the physical structure of neural circuits. Structural plasticity can include: formation of new dendritic spines stabilization of selected spines elimination of existing spines The circuit is therefore not anatomically fixed after development.

slides.title: The plasticity-stability dilemma
slides.text: The plasticity-stability dilemma Pure Hebbian plasticity contains a potential instability . If strong synapses are repeatedly strengthened because they are effective, they become even more likely to drive postsynaptic firing. Weak synapses may become progressively less effective. A useful nervous system must therefore be both: plastic enough to learn and stable enough to remain functional Without additional regulatory mechanisms, this positive feedback could push network activity toward runaway excitation or excessive silencing .

slides.title: Homeostatic plasticity
slides.text: Homeostatic plasticity Homeostatic plasticity regulates neural excitability so that activity remains within a functional range . If a neuron remains too inactive , synaptic drive can be increased. If it remains too active , synaptic drive can be reduced. Unlike Hebbian plasticity, the goal is not to select the most correlated input. The goal is to stabilize overall activity.

slides.title: Metaplasticity: plasticity of plasticity
slides.text: Metaplasticity: plasticity of plasticity Metaplasticity means that the recent history of a neuron changes how easily future plasticity can be induced . A classic example is the sliding threshold model : prolonged high activity can make further potentiation harder prolonged low activity can make potentiation easier The effect of a new activity pattern therefore depends partly on the previous activity state of the circuit .

slides.title: Hebbian and homeostatic plasticity solve different problems
slides.text: Hebbian and homeostatic plasticity solve different problems Hebbian plasticity Detects relationships between pre- and postsynaptic activity. Strengthens selected inputs that are effective at driving the postsynaptic neuron. Promotes selectivity and learning Homeostatic plasticity Compares ongoing activity with a functional activity range . Adjusts synaptic or intrinsic gain to compensate for persistent deviations. Promotes stability Neural circuits require both mechanisms : one allows representations to change, while the other prevents those changes from destabilizing the network.

slides.title: Plasticity persists in the adult brain
slides.text: Plasticity persists in the adult brain Development is a period of exceptionally high plasticity, but plasticity does not disappear in adulthood. Adult experience can modify: synaptic strength cortical representations dendritic spines functional connectivity behavioral performance The magnitude and mechanisms of plasticity depend on the circuit, the type of experience and the developmental stage.

slides.title: Structural plasticity: spine dynamics in adult visual cortex
slides.text: Structural plasticity: spine dynamics in adult visual cortex A small retinal lesion creates a scotoma and deprives the corresponding region of adult visual cortex of its normal input. The same dendritic spines can then be followed over time with two-photon imaging . Spine density remains approximately unchanged. Spine survival strongly decreases. The formation of new persistent spines increases. The number of spines is stable, but their turnover dramatically increases. The circuit is therefore being structurally reorganized without a net change in synapse density. Keck et al., 2008

slides.title: Motor learning reorganizes adult M1
slides.text: Motor learning reorganizes adult M1 Karni et al., 1995 Training Adults repeatedly practiced a specific sequence of rapid finger movements over several weeks. Measurement Task-related activity in primary motor cortex (M1) was measured using fMRI. Result After prolonged practice, the trained sequence produced an expanded M1 activation . The change persisted for months.

slides.title: Motor practice occludes PAS-induced potentiation
slides.text: Motor practice occludes PAS-induced potentiation Two ways to induce plasticity in human M1 Motor Practice (MP) Subjects repeatedly perform rapid thumb abduction movements for 30 min. After practice, TMS over M1 evokes a larger MEP in the trained thumb muscle. Paired Associative Stimulation Electrical stimulation of the median nerve is repeatedly paired with TMS over contralateral M1 . With the appropriate timing, PAS produces an LTP-like increase in MEP amplitude . Occlusion If subjects first perform motor practice , the subsequent potentiating effect of PAS is strongly reduced or absent. Interpretation Motor learning and PAS engage overlapping LTP-like plasticity mechanisms . Because motor practice has already potentiated the circuit, further potentiation by PAS is occluded .

slides.text: Development of Visual Function Sensory experience and critical periods Raffaele M Mazziotti, PhD Scuola di Psicologia, University of Florence

slides.title: Development of visual function
slides.text: Development of visual function The visual system is a useful model for understanding how development and experience interact to build neural function. Many visual pathways are already organized before normal vision begins. But the ability to see with adult precision develops gradually and depends on activity, sensory experience and circuit maturation .

slides.title: Anatomy of the eye and retina
slides.text: Anatomy of the eye and retina Light enters through the cornea and lens and is focused onto the retina . The retina is a specialized part of the nervous system that converts light into neural signals. Fovea : highest visual acuity Optic nerve : carries retinal output to the brain Vision begins with the transduction of light into neural activity in the retina.

slides.title: The retina performs neural computations
slides.text: The retina performs neural computations The retina is not simply a light detector: it is a layered neural circuit that begins processing visual information before it reaches the brain. Photoreceptors convert light into electrical signals ( cones and rods ). Bipolar cells transmit signals through the retina. Horizontal cells integrate activity across neighboring photoreceptors. Amacrine cells shape temporal and spatial responses. Retinal ganglion cells generate action potentials and form the optic nerve.

slides.title: From the retina to the visual cortex
slides.text: From the retina to the visual cortex Retinal ganglion cells provide the output of the retina. Their axons: form the optic nerve partially cross at the optic chiasm reach the LGN The LGN is a nucleus of the thalamus and acts as the major relay between the retina and visual cortex. From the LGN, thalamocortical projections carry visual information to the V1 .

slides.title: How is visual information processed?
slides.text: How is visual information processed? A fundamental concept in sensory systems is the receptive field . The receptive field of a neuron is the region of sensory space in which a stimulus can modify its activity . In the retina, signals from many photoreceptors are integrated onto a much smaller number of retinal ganglion cells . This convergence means that each ganglion cell integrates information from a region of the retina: its receptive field . Two major organizations are: Concentric ON-center / OFF-surround Concentric OFF-center / ON-surround

slides.title: Visual signals are segregated in the LGN
slides.text: Visual signals are segregated in the LGN After leaving the retina, axons of retinal ganglion cells form the optic nerve . At the optic chiasm : fibers from the nasal retina cross fibers from the temporal retina remain ipsilateral The signals then reach the LGN of the thalamus. Inside the LGN , information from the two eyes remains segregated into separate layers . Each LGN neuron therefore receives its main retinal input from one eye. LGN neurons retain concentric receptive fields similar to those of retinal ganglion cells: ON-center / OFF-surround or OFF-center / ON-surround . The signals from the two eyes are still largely separate at this stage of the visual pathway.

slides.title: From eye segregation to binocular integration
slides.text: From eye segregation to binocular integration In the LGN , signals from the two eyes remain segregated and organized in ocular dominance columns . When these projections reach V1 , they initially terminate in eye-specific territories. Thus, information arriving from the two eyes is still anatomically separated at the first cortical input stage. Within the visual cortex, however, cortical connections begin to combine information from the two eyes . V1 neurons can therefore be: monocular contralateral monocular ipsilateral binocular Binocular neurons respond to stimulation of either eye, although one eye may dominate the response. Across the population there is usually a contralateral-eye bias : neurons respond more to the eye opposite the recorded hemisphere.

slides.title: Receptive fields change in the visual cortex
slides.text: Receptive fields change in the visual cortex Retinal ganglion cells and LGN neurons have approximately circular center-surround receptive fields . In V1 , many neurons instead respond best to an elongated region of visual space . Because of this elongated organization, many cortical neurons become selective for the orientation of an edge or bar. A vertical receptive field, for example, responds strongly to a vertical edge but much less to the same edge rotated away from its preferred orientation. Video As visual information moves into cortex, the level of abstraction increases : neurons begin to represent features such as orientation , rather than simply local changes in luminance.

slides.title: How can an elongated receptive field emerge?
slides.text: How can an elongated receptive field emerge? Circular LGN receptive fields → spatially aligned convergence → elongated cortical receptive field → orientation selectivity A classical model proposed by Hubel and Wiesel explains cortical orientation selectivity through convergence . Several LGN neurons with circular center-surround receptive fields project onto the same cortical neuron. If those LGN receptive fields are aligned along a common axis, their combined input creates an elongated receptive field . The cortical neuron therefore responds preferentially when a bar or edge activates those inputs simultaneously. Classical feedforward model: Hubel & Wiesel 1962

slides.title: Two major streams of visual processing
slides.text: Two major streams of visual processing After V1 , visual information is distributed through at least two major cortical processing streams. As visual signals move beyond V1, the level of abstraction continues to increase : different cortical networks extract increasingly complex information about objects, space, and actions. Dorsal stream Projects mainly toward the parietal cortex . Processes information related to: motion spatial position visually guided action Often summarized as the “where / how” pathway . Ventral stream Projects mainly toward the temporal cortex . Processes information related to: shape color object identity Often summarized as the “what” pathway .

slides.title: Two major streams of visual processing
slides.text: Two major streams of visual processing

slides.title: Visual acuity
slides.text: Visual acuity Visual acuity is the ability to resolve fine spatial detail . Two nearby points can be distinguished only if the visual system preserves enough spatial information to represent them separately. Acuity is highest at the fovea and decreases toward the peripheral visual field. High acuity depends on several levels of the visual pathway: dense spacing of photoreceptors in the fovea low convergence from photoreceptors to RGC small receptive fields

slides.title: Spatial frequency
slides.text: Spatial frequency Spatial frequency describes how rapidly luminance changes across space . For a grating, it is usually expressed as cycles per degree (c/deg) of visual angle. The higher the spatial frequency, the finer the spatial detail that the visual system must resolve.

slides.title: Contrast sensitivity
slides.text: Contrast sensitivity Contrast sensitivity is the ability to detect differences in luminance . A stimulus may be large enough to resolve but still invisible if its contrast is too low. Contrast sensitivity depends strongly on spatial frequency : Human vision is usually most sensitive to intermediate spatial frequencies . The contrast sensitivity function (CSF) describes the minimum contrast needed to detect gratings of different spatial frequencies. Visual acuity mainly describes the finest resolvable detail, whereas contrast sensitivity describes visual performance across a much wider range of spatial scales.

slides.title: Depth perception
slides.text: Depth perception Binocular cues (near) Use information provided by the two eyes . The most important is retinal disparity : because the eyes occupy slightly different positions, the image projected onto each retina is not identical. The visual system compares these two images to estimate depth . Depth perception is therefore reconstructed from several visual cues rather than directly measured by a single receptor.

slides.title: Depth perception
slides.text: Depth perception Monocular cues (far) Depth can also be estimated from information available to one eye alone . These cues are particularly important for objects that are farther away , where binocular disparity becomes small. Depth perception is therefore reconstructed from several visual cues rather than directly measured by a single receptor.

slides.title: Monocular cues to depth
slides.text: Monocular cues to depth The visual system can infer three-dimensional structure from patterns contained in a single retinal image. Perspective Parallel lines converge with distance and objects become progressively smaller in the retinal image. Occlusion If one object blocks part of another, the blocking object is interpreted as being closer . Relative size For objects of similar expected size, the object producing the smaller retinal image is generally interpreted as farther away . Shading The distribution of light and shadow provides information about three-dimensional shape. The same pattern can appear convex or concave depending on the assumed direction of illumination.

slides.title: The visual system at birth
slides.text: The visual system at birth Anatomically advanced major visual pathways are present retina and dLGN are organized thalamocortical projections have reached V1 substantial cortical organization is already present Functionally immature low visual acuity low contrast sensitivity immature focusing immature control of eye movements A circuit can be present before it performs at the adult level.

slides.title: Development of visual acuity
slides.text: Development of visual acuity At birth, visual acuity is approximately 40 times poorer than in adults . Its development is limited by both peripheral and central maturation. Peripheral factors The retina is still immature at birth. A major limitation is the maturation of photoreceptors , especially in the fovea: photoreceptors become more densely packed outer segments elongate retinal sampling becomes more precise Central factors Visual acuity also depends on maturation of the LGN and V1 . During development: inhibitory circuits mature receptive fields become smaller and more selective cortical processing becomes more spatially precise The increase in visual acuity during development reflects the combined maturation of the retina , thalamus , and visual cortex .

slides.title: Visual acuity progressively matures during childhood
slides.text: Visual acuity progressively matures during childhood Visual acuity improves very rapidly during the first year of life , but development continues for several years. By approximately 5-6 years of age , high-contrast visual acuity approaches adult-like values , although the exact age depends on the task and measurement used. The developmental improvement reflects the progressive maturation of the entire visual pathway: retina -> LGN -> V1

slides.title: Photoreceptors mature after birth
slides.text: Photoreceptors mature after birth By approximately 4-6 years of age , foveal cone density and morphology approach adult values. During development, especially in the fovea , photoreceptors: become smaller and more densely packed elongate their outer segments become more regularly organized This increases the number of photoreceptors sampling a given region of visual space. Denser photoreceptor packing provides finer spatial sampling of the retinal image and contributes to the developmental improvement in visual acuity.

slides.title: Neural activity begins before vision
slides.text: Neural activity begins before vision Before normal visual experience begins, the immature retina is already electrically active . Groups of neighboring retinal ganglion cells become active together in spontaneous patterns called retinal waves . These waves propagate through developing visual pathways and provide patterned activity before the animal can use vision normally. Mooney et al., 1996 Video

slides.title: Retinal waves provide structured information
slides.text: Retinal waves provide structured information Nearby retinal neurons tend to be active at similar times. Their activity is therefore correlated in space and time . Activity from different retinal regions is less strongly correlated. This creates information about which neurons belong together even before patterned vision. Spontaneous activity can therefore contribute to refinement of retinotopic and eye-specific connections before sensory experience begins.

slides.title: Retinal activity helps organize thalamic connections
slides.text: Retinal activity helps organize thalamic connections If spontaneous activity in one eye is blocked with TTX , the normal eye-specific projection from that retina to the LGN fails to develop correctly. In the normal condition, inputs from the two eyes form distinct territories in the thalamus. After TTX injection into one eye, the territory normally occupied by that eye is strongly reduced or can disappear. Spontaneous retinal activity is therefore required for normal refinement and segregation of retinogeniculate connections.

slides.title: Contrast sensitivity develops during childhood
slides.text: Contrast sensitivity develops during childhood During development, the contrast sensitivity function progressively changes: sensitivity to contrast increases progressively higher spatial frequencies become detectable the range of spatial frequencies processed efficiently becomes broader Development does not simply increase visual acuity: it improves sensitivity across the entire range of spatial frequencies. The maturation of contrast sensitivity depends on the development of inhibitory circuitry in V1. Inhibition does not simply suppress visual activity: it refines the representation , helping cortical neurons discriminate contrast more precisely.

slides.title: If wiring begins before vision, what is experience for?
slides.text: If wiring begins before vision, what is experience for? Molecular guidance and spontaneous activity can establish a surprisingly organized initial circuit. But normal visual experience is required to refine, stabilize and calibrate that circuit for the statistics of the real visual world. This is where developmental neuroplasticity becomes especially important.

slides.title: Critical periods
slides.text: Critical periods A critical period is a developmental window during which particular neural circuits are especially sensitive to experience . Experience during this period can produce large and persistent changes in circuit organization and function. The same manipulation later in life usually produces a much smaller effect. The end of a critical period does not mean that plasticity disappears completely. It means that the rules and magnitude of plasticity change with maturation.

slides.title: Human evidence: congenital cataract
slides.text: Human evidence: congenital cataract A dense congenital cataract prevents patterned visual information from reaching the retina normally during early development. Removing the cataract early generally allows substantially better visual development than restoring patterned vision only after prolonged deprivation. The outcome depends not only on whether visual input is restored, but also on when it is restored.

slides.title: Case study: S.B.
slides.text: Case study: S.B. S.B. experienced severe visual deprivation from early life (3 years old) and underwent surgery only in adulthood, at about 50 years of age . After sight was restored: visual acuity improved, but remained far below normal recognition of novel objects remained difficult stereopsis did not develop face perception was impaired perception of complex forms remained strongly limited Restoring visual input in adulthood was not sufficient to produce normal visual perception . Some visual abilities require appropriate sensory experience during development.

slides.title: Amblyopia: abnormal experience changes cortical function
slides.text: Amblyopia: abnormal experience changes cortical function Amblyopia is reduced visual function caused by abnormal visual experience during development , not simply by damage to the eye or retina. Common developmental causes include: unilateral cataract strabismus strong unequal refractive error between the eyes If the two eyes provide persistently unequal or mismatched input, cortical circuits become biased toward the more effective input.

slides.title: Hubel and Wiesel: monocular deprivation
slides.text: Hubel and Wiesel: monocular deprivation A classic test of experience-dependent development Manipulation One eye of a young animal is closed during a period of early visual development. Measurement After deprivation, responses of individual neurons in V1 are measured separately through each eye. Result Many cortical neurons become dominated by the nondeprived eye and respond weakly or not at all to the deprived eye. Wiesel & Hubel, 1963

slides.title: Ocular dominance in normal visual cortex
slides.text: Ocular dominance in normal visual cortex Many neurons in binocular visual cortex can be driven by both eyes, although individual neurons may prefer one eye. In species such as cats and primates, geniculocortical inputs from the two eyes form alternating ocular dominance columns , particularly in layer IV of V1. Normal binocular vision therefore depends on coordinated convergence of the two eyes onto cortical circuits .

slides.title: Monocular deprivation changes cortical responses
slides.text: Monocular deprivation changes cortical responses Before deprivation, V1 contains neurons spanning a broad range of ocular preferences , including many binocular neurons. After deprivation during the critical period, the distribution shifts dramatically toward the open eye .

slides.title: Functional change becomes anatomical change
slides.text: Functional change becomes anatomical change After prolonged monocular deprivation , the shift in ocular dominance is accompanied by structural reorganization of the visual pathway. The ocular dominance columns representing the deprived eye become smaller, while columns driven by the open eye expand. At the same time, geniculocortical axon arbors serving the deprived eye shrink, whereas those serving the non-deprived eye occupy more cortical territory. Prolonged abnormal visual experience can therefore transform an initial functional imbalance into a stable anatomical reorganization of developing visual cortex.

slides.title: Why is monocular deprivation so powerful?
slides.text: Why is monocular deprivation so powerful? The effect is not explained simply by a lack of visual stimulation. During monocular deprivation, the two eyes compete under strongly unequal conditions: open eye -> effective patterned activity deprived eye -> weak or abnormal drive

slides.title: Strabismus reveals another rule
slides.text: Strabismus reveals another rule In strabismus , both eyes can remain active at the same level, but the two retinal images are spatially misaligned . Activity from corresponding points in the two eyes is therefore less consistently correlated . The result is a strong reduction in binocular cortical neurons and impaired stereoscopic vision. Normal binocular development requires coordinated activity from the two eyes.

slides.title: Correlation matters, not activity alone
slides.text: Correlation matters, not activity alone Controlling the temporal relationship between the two eyes Question Is activity sufficient, or must activity from the two eyes be temporally coordinated? Manipulation Retinal activity is experimentally controlled so that the two optic pathways are activated either synchronously or asynchronously . Result Synchronous activity favors binocular convergence, whereas strongly asynchronous activity favors more monocular organization. The temporal relationship between inputs provides information about which connections should be associated .

slides.title: Critical-period plasticity changes with age
slides.text: Critical-period plasticity changes with age The response to the same sensory manipulation depends strongly on developmental age. During the critical period, brief monocular deprivation can produce a large ocular-dominance shift. Before the window is fully open or after it has largely closed, the same deprivation produces a smaller effect. Critical periods therefore reflect developmental regulation of the capacity for experience-dependent circuit change .

slides.title: Critical period closure reduces cortical plasticity
slides.text: Critical period closure reduces cortical plasticity During the critical period , visual cortex is highly susceptible to activity-dependent modification. At the synaptic level, this is accompanied by a strong capacity to induce LTP . As development proceeds and the critical period closes: LTP induction becomes progressively less effective the same stimulation produces smaller potentiation cortical circuits become increasingly resistant to long-lasting modification The closure of the critical period is therefore accompanied by a decrease in the capacity to induce LTP : synaptic connections become progressively more stable and less easily modified by experience.

slides.title: Sensory experience helps regulate the window
slides.text: Sensory experience helps regulate the window The timing of critical-period closure is not determined by chronological age alone. In animal models, rearing in darkness can delay aspects of visual cortical maturation and prolong the period during which strong experience-dependent plasticity can be expressed. Experience is both a driver of plasticity and one of the signals that contributes to circuit maturation.

slides.title: Inhibition helps open and regulate critical-period plasticity
slides.text: Inhibition helps open and regulate critical-period plasticity One of the major developmental changes in visual cortex is maturation of GABAergic inhibition . Experiments manipulating GABAergic transmission showed that a sufficient level of cortical inhibition is required for normal ocular-dominance plasticity to emerge. The critical period is therefore not simply a time when the cortex is “more excitable”. It depends on maturation of a specific excitatory-inhibitory circuit state . Hensch et al., 1998 | Fagiolini & Hensch, 2000

slides.title: BDNF can change the timing of the critical period
slides.text: BDNF can change the timing of the critical period BDNF promotes maturation of cortical inhibitory circuitry during development. When BDNF expression is increased precociously in mouse visual cortex: GABAergic maturation occurs earlier visual functions mature earlier susceptibility to monocular deprivation shifts to an earlier age Changing circuit maturation can therefore shift the timing of developmental plasticity . Huang et al., 1999

slides.title: BDNF anticipates the closure of the critical period in V1
slides.text: BDNF anticipates the closure of the critical period in V1 Cortical plasticity Increased BDNF accelerates maturation of GABAergic inhibition . As a consequence: ocular-dominance plasticity appears earlier sensitivity to monocular deprivation peaks earlier the critical period also closes earlier The period of high cortical plasticity is therefore shifted to a younger age. Visual function Visual functions such as visual acuity also mature earlier in BDNF-overexpressing animals. However, the final level reached is the same as in WT animals. BDNF changes the timing of maturation , rather than the final capability.

slides.title: The mature circuit becomes harder to modify
slides.text: The mature circuit becomes harder to modify Critical-period closure also involves the accumulation of molecular and structural constraints that stabilize mature circuits. Perineuronal nets (PNNs) are extracellular-matrix structures that accumulate around subsets of neurons, particularly many parvalbumin interneurons. These structures are associated with increased circuit stability and reduced juvenile-like plasticity.

slides.title: Removing a structural brake can restore plasticity
slides.text: Removing a structural brake can restore plasticity Reopening ocular-dominance plasticity in adult visual cortex Manipulation Chondroitinase ABC is used to degrade chondroitin-sulfate proteoglycans in the mature extracellular matrix. Test Adult animals then undergo monocular deprivation, which normally produces little ocular-dominance shift after the critical period. Result Ocular-dominance plasticity reappears in the adult visual cortex. Critical-period closure is therefore an actively maintained stable state , and not irreversible. Pizzorusso et al., 2002

slides.title: Parental Care and Attachment
slides.text: Parental Care and Attachment How early social experience shapes the developing brain Raffaele M Mazziotti, PhD Scuola di Psicologia, University of Florence

slides.title: Parental care is part of development
slides.text: Parental care is part of development Parental care is a social behavior that increases the probability that offspring survive, grow, and acquire the skills needed for independent life. Sustenance and protection Parents can provide: food and warmth protection from predators transport and shelter physiological regulation Learning and experience Parents can also provide: opportunities for exploration social interaction information about the environment species-specific skills and behaviors

slides.title: Why does parental care evolve?
slides.text: Why does parental care evolve? Parental care can be energetically expensive . Feeding, protecting, carrying, or defending offspring can reduce the parent’s time and resources for other activities. However, parental investment can increase fitness by increasing the probability that offspring survive and eventually reproduce. The evolutionary benefit is therefore indirect through the success of the offspring. Parental behavior reflects a trade-off between the cost of investment and the benefit to offspring survival and reproductive success .

slides.title: Different reproductive strategies
slides.text: Different reproductive strategies High investment Some species produce relatively few offspring and invest heavily in each one. Parental care may include prolonged feeding, protection, teaching, and social interaction. Low investment Other species produce many offspring and invest less in each individual. Survival depends more strongly on producing large numbers of offspring. The classical r/K framework describes these as opposite ends of a continuum . Modern life-history theory treats reproductive strategies as more complex than a strict two-category division.

slides.title: Attachment
slides.text: Attachment What is attachment? Attachment is a stable emotional bond between an infant and a caregiver. It motivates the young animal to stay close to the caregiver, seek protection, and use the caregiver as a secure base for exploration. Why does it evolve? Attachment is especially important in species with high parental investment. When offspring depend on care, feeding, protection, and learning, staying close to the caregiver increases survival. Attachment is not simply “love” or “affection”. It is a biological and behavioral system that regulates proximity, safety, stress, and exploration.

slides.title: Harlow: is attachment simply about food?
slides.text: Harlow: is attachment simply about food? Surrogate-mother experiments in infant rhesus monkeys Question Is the infant’s attachment to the mother produced mainly because the mother provides food ? Manipulation Infant monkeys were given access to two surrogate mothers: a wire surrogate a soft cloth surrogate Observation The infants spent much more time clinging to the cloth surrogate , even when food was delivered by the wire surrogate. Harlow, 1958 - The Nature of Love

slides.title: Contact comfort is a powerful attachment signal
slides.text: Contact comfort is a powerful attachment signal Harlow called the preference for the soft surrogate contact comfort . The result challenged the idea that attachment is simply a secondary consequence of feeding. For infant primates, physical contact, warmth, and security are themselves powerful reinforcers .

slides.title: The caregiver can become a secure base
slides.text: The caregiver can become a secure base When placed in a novel environment without the familiar surrogate, infant monkeys showed: less exploration more distress freezing or withdrawal When the cloth surrogate was available, the infants used it as a source of security and explored the environment more readily. Video Video Attachment does not only keep the infant close to the caregiver. It can also create a secure base from which the environment can be explored.

slides.title: Early social deprivation has lasting effects
slides.text: Early social deprivation has lasting effects Harlow’s later social-isolation experiments showed that severe early deprivation can produce persistent abnormalities in social and emotional behavior. The historical experiments are scientifically important but would raise major ethical concerns under modern standards for animal research. The broader principle is that early social experience can shape later behavior long after the original experience has ended .

slides.title: Recognition is bidirectional and multisensory
slides.text: Recognition is bidirectional and multisensory Successful parental care requires both the caregiver and the offspring to identify and respond to relevant social signals. In many rodents , olfactory cues are especially important. Newborn pups use maternal odors to orient toward the mother and the nest. In primates , visual, tactile, and vocal signals make a major contribution to parent-offspring interaction. There is no single universal “maternal stimulus”: different species weight sensory channels differently.

slides.title: Imprinting: learning very early in life
slides.text: Imprinting: learning very early in life In some species, young animals rapidly learn the characteristics of a caregiver or another salient stimulus shortly after birth or hatching. This form of early learning is called imprinting . Classic examples come from precocial birds, in which newly hatched chicks or goslings develop a strong tendency to follow the object to which they were exposed early in life. Imprinting shows that social preferences can be strongly shaped by experience during a restricted developmental window .

slides.title: Imprinting occurs during a sensitive period
slides.text: Imprinting occurs during a sensitive period Konrad Lorenz originally described imprinting as occurring within a sharply defined critical period and as essentially irreversible. Later work showed a more flexible picture: the effective window can vary with experience preferences can sometimes be modified natural stimuli often retain privileged status It is therefore usually more accurate to think of imprinting as learning with a particularly strong sensitive period .

slides.title: Imprinting changes the developing brain
slides.text: Imprinting changes the developing brain In domestic chicks, a forebrain region now called the intermediate medial mesopallium (IMM) is strongly involved in visual imprinting. Learning changes neuronal responses and synaptic properties in this region. Early attachment-related learning is not merely behavioral: it is accompanied by experience-dependent modification of neural circuits . Horn, 1998

slides.title: Mammalian attachment also depends on learning
slides.text: Mammalian attachment also depends on learning In mammals, attachment is not produced by a single hard-wired image of the caregiver. Young mammals learn combinations of sensory cues associated with the caregiver. In newborn rats, odor learning is especially important because pups must orient toward the mother before vision and hearing are fully functional. The developing nervous system is temporarily configured to learn caregiver-related cues very efficiently.

slides.title: Norepinephrine supports early odor learning
slides.text: Norepinephrine supports early odor learning In neonatal rats, maternal odors can acquire strong positive value through early experience. Norepinephrine released from the locus coeruleus strongly modulates plasticity in the olfactory bulb . Pairing an odor with maternal-like tactile stimulation can produce a learned preference for that odor, but only in a restricted time window. Early attachment learning depends on special developmental states of neuromodulatory and sensory circuits .

slides.title: Mothers also learn to recognize their offspring
slides.text: Mothers also learn to recognize their offspring In sheep, the mother forms a selective recognition of her own lamb within the first hours after birth. This recognition depends strongly on olfactory information . Noradrenergic signaling in the maternal olfactory bulb contributes to formation of this memory. Blocking this signaling interferes with selective recognition of the lamb. Parent-offspring attachment is bidirectional : the young learn the caregiver, and the caregiver can learn the young.

slides.title: Maternal behavior in rodents can be quantified
slides.text: Maternal behavior in rodents can be quantified Rodent maternal behavior consists of recognizable behavioral modules: pup retrieval licking and grooming arched-back nursing nest building > > > Because these behaviors are stereotyped and quantifiable , rats and mice provide powerful experimental models for studying the neurobiology of parental care.

slides.title: Pregnancy prepares the maternal brain
slides.text: Pregnancy prepares the maternal brain The endocrine state of pregnancy helps prepare the nervous system for the rapid onset of maternal behavior around parturition. Important signals include: estradiol progesterone prolactin oxytocin These hormones do not act as a simple on/off switch. They modify the responsiveness of neural circuits that process offspring-related sensory signals and motivation.

slides.title: The medial preoptic area coordinates parental behavior
slides.text: The medial preoptic area coordinates parental behavior The medial preoptic area (MPOA) of the hypothalamus is a major node in the neural circuitry controlling parental behavior. The MPOA integrates: hormonal state sensory signals from offspring motivational and reward-related information Disrupting MPOA function strongly impairs maternal behavior in rodents.

slides.title: Hormones facilitate care, but experience also matters
slides.text: Hormones facilitate care, but experience also matters Virgin female rats do not normally show the same rapid maternal response as females around parturition. However, repeated exposure to pups can gradually induce maternal behavior even without pregnancy. This phenomenon is often called maternal sensitization . Removing olfactory input accelerates the onset of maternal behavior in virgin rats.

slides.title: Early maternal care shapes the stress system
slides.text: Early maternal care shapes the stress system Rat mothers naturally differ in the frequency of behaviors such as: licking/grooming and arched-back nursing . These naturally occurring differences are associated with long-lasting differences in the offspring’s: stress reactivity exploratory behavior HPA-axis regulation Early caregiving becomes part of the developmental environment that calibrates the offspring’s future response to stress. This makes rodents a valuable model for studying how variation in early maternal care influences developmental trajectories and adult outcomes.

slides.title: High maternal care changes HPA-axis regulation
slides.text: High maternal care changes HPA-axis regulation Offspring receiving relatively high LG/ABN show, on average: higher hippocampal glucocorticoid receptor (GR) expression stronger glucocorticoid negative feedback smaller ACTH and corticosterone responses to acute stress The effect of early care is therefore not only behavioral: it changes the physiological regulation of the stress response . Liu et al., 1997

slides.title: Cross-fostering separates genes from caregiving
slides.text: Cross-fostering separates genes from caregiving Cross-fostering between mothers with different caregiving styles Question Are differences in offspring stress responses inherited genetically, or produced by the maternal environment? Manipulation Newborn pups from one mother are raised by a foster mother showing a different level of LG/ABN . Result Adult behavior and stress physiology tend to resemble the style associated with the rearing mother , rather than simply the biological mother. Francis et al., 1999

slides.title: Cross-fostering separates genes from caregiving
slides.text: Cross-fostering separates genes from caregiving

slides.title: Parental style can be transmitted without changing DNA sequence
slides.text: Parental style can be transmitted without changing DNA sequence Female offspring raised by high-LG mothers tend to provide higher levels of maternal care when they later become mothers themselves. Cross-fostering can shift this pattern. This demonstrates a form of nongenomic transmission across generations. Behavior can be transmitted across generations through developmental experience , even when the DNA sequence itself is unchanged.

slides.title: Epigenetics: regulating genes without changing DNA sequence
slides.text: Epigenetics: regulating genes without changing DNA sequence Epigenetics Epigenetics refers to molecular mechanisms that regulate gene activity without changing the DNA sequence. These mechanisms help cells decide which genes are accessible, active, or silent. Two key mechanisms DNA methylation Histone modifications Both influence how easily transcription machinery can access DNA. The genome is the same, but epigenetic marks help determine how strongly different genes are expressed.

slides.title: DNA methylation and histone modifications
slides.text: DNA methylation and histone modifications DNA methylation Small chemical groups called methyl groups are added to DNA, often at cytosine bases. In segments of DNA called CpG islands High DNA methylation near a gene promoter is usually associated with reduced gene expression . Histone modifications DNA is wrapped around histone proteins. Chemical modifications to histone tails can make chromatin more open or more compact, changing gene accessibility . In simple terms: DNA methylation often acts like a “do not read” signal Histone modifications can open or close the chromatin structure, regulating the accessibility to specific genes.

slides.title: DNA methylation and histone modifications
slides.text: DNA methylation and histone modifications DNA methylation Histone modifications

slides.title: Early care can modify gene expression epigenetically
slides.text: Early care can modify gene expression epigenetically Maternal care influences regulation of the hippocampal glucocorticoid receptor (GR) gene. Particularly through tactile stimulation (licking/grroming) High maternal care is associated with: reduced DNA methylation at a GR promoter greater access of transcription factors such as NGFI-A / EGR1 increased GR expression ( Nr3c1 is the gene) An early social experience can become biologically persistent by altering how strongly genes are expressed , without changing the DNA sequence. Weaver et al., 2004

slides.title: Epigenetic programming is stable, but not necessarily permanent
slides.text: Epigenetic programming is stable, but not necessarily permanent The epigenetic differences associated with early maternal care can persist into adulthood. In experimental animals, pharmacological manipulation of chromatin regulation can modify some of these molecular differences even later in life. Epigenetic does not mean genetically predetermined or absolutely irreversible. It describes persistent regulation of gene expression that can remain responsive to later biological and environmental influences .

slides.title: Brief handling and prolonged separation are not equivalent
slides.text: Brief handling and prolonged separation are not equivalent Brief handling Short separations can increase maternal interaction after reunion and, in some rodent paradigms, are associated with reduced later stress reactivity. Prolonged maternal separation Longer repeated separations can act as early-life stressors and can produce persistent changes in stress-related physiology and behavior. The effect of early separation depends on duration, age, strain, housing, and what happens when mother and pups are reunited .

slides.title: Early experience changes probabilities, not destiny
slides.text: Early experience changes probabilities, not destiny Early parental care can have long-lasting effects because it acts while neural, endocrine, and epigenetic systems are developing. But later experience continues to matter. Social environment, enrichment, stress, and new relationships can interact with the developmental state created earlier in life. Early experience can bias developmental trajectories without rigidly determining a single adult outcome.

slides.title: Prenatal Sensory and Cognitive Development
slides.text: Prenatal Sensory and Cognitive Development Sensory and cognitive functions in the fetus Raffaele M Mazziotti, PhD Scuola di Psicologia, University of Florence

slides.title: Development begins before birth
slides.text: Development begins before birth Birth is an important biological transition, but it is not the beginning of sensory and cognitive development . During prenatal life, the nervous system progressively becomes able to: detect information from the body and the environment modify behavior in response to stimulation learn from repeated experience retain some information across time The abilities observed in newborns therefore have important prenatal origins .

slides.title: How can we study the fetus?
slides.text: How can we study the fetus? The fetus cannot provide verbal reports or perform conventional behavioral tasks. Behavioral measures Researchers can measure: body and eye movements with ultrasound changes in fetal heart rate orienting or motor responses to stimulation habituation to repeated stimuli Brain activity Prenatal neural responses can also be studied using methods such as: fetal MEG fetal fMRI sensory-evoked responses Fetal perception is inferred from changes in behavior, physiology, or brain activity produced by controlled stimulation.

slides.title: Sensory development is continuous across birth
slides.text: Sensory development is continuous across birth Before birth The fetus experiences a restricted but structured sensory environment. Sensory systems become functional at different times and begin modifying neural activity. After birth The quantity and diversity of sensory input increase dramatically. The same developing systems continue to learn and reorganize. Birth changes the environment, but development itself is continuous .

slides.title: Sensory systems do not mature at the same time
slides.text: Sensory systems do not mature at the same time Earlier functional development touch and somatosensation vestibular and proprioceptive signals chemosensory experience Later functional development hearing becomes increasingly effective during gestation vision becomes responsive much later and receives no patterned stimulation in utero The prenatal sensory environment is not silent or empty : the fetus receives continuous tactile, vestibular, chemical, and acoustic information.

slides.title: Touch develops early
slides.text: Touch develops early Somatosensation is the earliest sensory systems to become functional. Responses to tactile stimulation begin in restricted regions of the body and progressively spread as the peripheral and central somatosensory systems mature. By the second trimester , fetuses show an increasingly rich repertoire of: self-touch contact with the uterine wall hand-to-face movements responses to mechanical stimulation Prenatal touch is both externally generated and self-generated .

slides.title: Fetal movements become increasingly organized
slides.text: Fetal movements become increasingly organized As gestation progresses, fetal movements become more coordinated. Hand movements increasingly target specific regions such as the mouth and face . 4D ultrasound studies suggest thatstarting from 32 weeks some movements become increasingly anticipatory: mouth movements can begin before the hand reaches the mouth. The developing fetus is not simply producing random movements: sensorimotor organization progressively emerges before birth . Reissland et al., 2014

slides.title: The fetus can respond to touch through the maternal abdomen
slides.text: The fetus can respond to touch through the maternal abdomen Maternal abdominal touch and fetal behavior Manipulation The mother’s abdomen is touched while fetal movements are monitored with 4D ultrasound . Measurement Researchers quantify movements such as: self-touch reaching toward the uterine wall head and arm movements Result Fetal behavior changes during maternal touch, and the pattern of response depends on gestational age . Marx & Nagy, 2015 | Marx & Nagy, 2017

slides.title: Taste and smell begin before birth
slides.text: Taste and smell begin before birth The fetus repeatedly swallows amniotic fluid . This fluid contains chemical compounds derived from: maternal diet maternal metabolism the fetal environment Chemosensory systems can therefore sample information that changes with the mother’s diet. For the fetus, taste and smell are closely linked components of a broader chemosensory experience .

slides.title: Fetuses discriminate flavors before birth
slides.text: Fetuses discriminate flavors before birth Direct evidence of fetal responses to flavors Exposure At 32–36 weeks of gestation, mothers consumed a capsule containing: carrot flavor kale flavor or no flavor ( control ) About 20 minutes later, fetal facial movements were recorded with 4D ultrasound . Measurement Researchers quantified specific facial movements and combinations of movements. They compared 35 carrot-exposed , 34 kale-exposed , and 30 control fetuses. Result Carrot exposure increased movements contributing to a “laughter-face” pattern. Kale exposure increased movements contributing to a “cry-face” pattern. The two flavors therefore produced different fetal facial responses . Ustun et al., 2022 — Psychological Science

slides.title: Fetuses discriminate flavors before birth
slides.text: Fetuses discriminate flavors before birth Human fetuses can sense and discriminate flavors transferred from the maternal diet before birth. The facial patterns indicate differential responses, but they should not be interpreted as evidence that the fetus consciously experiences “happiness” or “disgust”.

slides.title: Newborns recognize prenatal odors
slides.text: Newborns recognize prenatal odors Newborns preferentially orient toward the odor of their own amniotic fluid compared with unfamiliar amniotic-fluid odor. This preference is present very soon after birth, before extensive postnatal learning can occur. The result provides evidence that the fetus can detect, encode, and later recognize chemosensory information from the prenatal environment. Schaal et al., 1998

slides.title: Prenatal chemosensory learning can bridge birth
slides.text: Prenatal chemosensory learning can bridge birth Chemical continuity exists between prenatal and postnatal life. Some odor and flavor compounds present in amniotic fluid can also be present around the maternal breast and in breast milk. Birth changes the environment dramatically, but familiar prenatal sensory signals can help create continuity across the transition . This is one example of how prenatal learning can influence behavior immediately after birth.

slides.title: The womb is an acoustic environment
slides.text: The womb is an acoustic environment The fetus is continuously exposed to sound generated both inside and outside the maternal body. Important sources include: maternal heartbeat and respiration movement and digestive sounds the mother’s voice external speech and environmental sounds Maternal tissues and amniotic fluid modify external sounds , especially attenuating higher frequencies, but temporal and prosodic information can still reach the fetus.

slides.title: Auditory responses emerge before birth
slides.text: Auditory responses emerge before birth During the second half of gestation, acoustic stimulation can produce measurable changes in: fetal heart rate body movement brain responses Responses become faster and more reliable with maturation. The auditory system is already processing environmental information before birth . Draganova et al., 2018

slides.title: The mother’s voice is a special prenatal stimulus
slides.text: The mother’s voice is a special prenatal stimulus The maternal voice reaches the fetus through both: external air conduction vibrations transmitted through the mother’s body This makes the mother’s voice one of the most frequent and biologically relevant complex sounds in the prenatal environment. After birth, newborns can distinguish the maternal voice from unfamiliar female voices. DeCasper & Fifer, 1980

slides.title: Recognition of the maternal voice begins prenatally
slides.text: Recognition of the maternal voice begins prenatally Voice recognition around birth Prenatal exposure The fetus repeatedly hears the mother’s voice during gestation. The baby behavior is monitored using non-nutritive sucking. Newborn test Newborn behavior is used to compare responses to the mother’s voice and an unfamiliar female voice. Result Newborns preferentially respond to or work to hear the maternal voice . Because the preference is present immediately after birth, it provides evidence that voice learning begins prenatally .

slides.title: Vision develops in a very different environment
slides.text: Vision develops in a very different environment Compared with touch, hearing, and chemosensation, vision receives relatively little structured stimulation before birth. The uterus is dark and maternal tissues strongly attenuate incoming light. Nevertheless, sufficient external light can reach the fetus, especially late in gestation. Late-gestation fetuses can show behavioral and neural responses to intense light stimulation. The fetal visual system is functional before birth , but normal patterned visual experience begins mainly after birth.

slides.title: Fetuses respond to light late in gestation
slides.text: Fetuses respond to light late in gestation External light stimulation Stimulus A controlled light source is presented through the maternal abdomen. Measurement Researchers monitor fetal: heart rate head or eye movements brain activity Result Late-gestation fetuses can show reproducible responses to visual stimulation. Kiuchi et al., 2000 | Fulford et al., 2003

slides.title: Fetal vision should not be overinterpreted
slides.text: Fetal vision should not be overinterpreted Experiments can demonstrate that the late fetus: detects sufficiently intense light changes behavior in response to visual stimulation can produce stimulus-related eye and head movements But this does not imply that prenatal vision resembles normal postnatal vision. Natural intrauterine visual input is weak and poorly structured. A sensory system can be physiologically responsive before it receives the rich environmental input required for mature perception .

slides.title: How can we test cognition before birth?
slides.text: How can we test cognition before birth? Cognition cannot be assessed in the fetus in the same way as in children or adults. The clearest evidence comes from simple forms of learning and memory . Two especially useful approaches are: Habituation Does the response decrease when the same stimulus is repeated? Recognition / retention Does previous exposure change the response when the stimulus is presented again later?

slides.title: Habituation is a simple form of learning
slides.text: Habituation is a simple form of learning When a stimulus is presented repeatedly, the response often becomes progressively smaller. This decrease is called habituation . Habituation shows that the nervous system is not merely detecting the stimulus. It is changing its response as a consequence of previous stimulation . Habituation is therefore one of the simplest experimental demonstrations of learning.

slides.title: Human fetuses can habituate
slides.text: Human fetuses can habituate Repeated vibroacoustic stimulation Stimulus The same vibrotactile or vibroacoustic stimulus is repeatedly presented. Observation The fetal motor response progressively decreases across repeated presentations. Interpretation The decrement is consistent with habituation , a basic form of learning. Leader et al., 1982

slides.title: Fetal learning becomes more efficient with development
slides.text: Fetal learning becomes more efficient with development Studies of fetal habituation show that responses change with gestational age . Older fetuses generally: respond more consistently habituate more efficiently retain information for longer intervals The development of learning and memory parallels the maturation of the fetal nervous system .

slides.title: The newborn can reveal prenatal memory
slides.text: The newborn can reveal prenatal memory Some prenatal learning is easiest to detect after birth . Newborn preferences can reveal familiarity with: maternal voice native-language rhythm previously heard speech prenatal odors and flavors Because these effects are measurable immediately after birth, they cannot be explained entirely by postnatal experience. The newborn arrives with a history of sensory experience .

slides.title: Prenatal learning prepares the transition to postnatal life
slides.text: Prenatal learning prepares the transition to postnatal life Prenatal learning does not mean that the fetus possesses mature adult cognition. Instead, it allows the developing nervous system to extract regularities from the prenatal environment. These regularities can make biologically important stimuli familiar before birth: the mother’s voice characteristics of language maternal odors and flavors Learning before birth can prepare behavior for the environment encountered immediately after birth .

slides.title: What can we conclude about fetal cognition?
slides.text: What can we conclude about fetal cognition? There is strong evidence that the human fetus can: detect several classes of sensory information discriminate some stimulus properties habituate to repeated stimulation learn recurring sensory patterns retain some information across time These results should not be interpreted as evidence for adult-like thought, language, or conscious understanding. Fetal cognition is best understood as the emergence of basic learning, memory, discrimination, and sensorimotor organization .
